concepts.title: Your First Running Program
concepts.summary: Write Main.java, compile it, and run its main method.
explanation: Java source is plain text. In this course the file is Main.java and its public class is Main. The names must agree. The compiler javac checks the source and produces Main.class. The java command runs that compiled class; do not pass Main.java to this course’s compiled-run command.

Execution starts in public static void main(String[] args). Braces group the class body and method body. The print statement belongs inside main and ends with a semicolon. For now, keep the entry-point words intact; methods and static will get their own lessons later.

The Code Bench performs compile then run for you. A successful run is not the same as a correct task answer. Check stdout against the requested text. Compiler errors happen before the program can run.
outcomes: Locate the entry point and its statement.
Compile and run a correctly named Main class.

concepts.title: Output, Lines & Comments
concepts.summary: Make a readable receipt without confusing code with output.
explanation: println prints its argument followed by a line break. print does not add a break. Two print calls can therefore share a line. Use spaces and labels deliberately: a program can run successfully while its output is hard to read.

A // comment ends at the end of its source line. The compiler ignores comments. Use a comment to explain a decision, not to repeat every statement. Text inside double quotes is a String literal, even when it contains symbols that look like code.
outcomes: Choose print versus println for a layout.

concepts.title: Plan Inputs, Work & Output
concepts.summary: Design a small request before choosing Java syntax.
explanation: Start with the result the user needs. Then list the inputs that determine it. Processing connects those inputs to the result. For a ticket total, count and unit price are inputs, multiplication is processing, and total is output.

A plan is not yet Java code. Use ordinary words here. Record units and assumptions: a count is a whole number; a fare rate is money per distance unit. State the valid input range, even before you know how to enforce it in Java.

An example tests whether the plan is unambiguous. A valid case, a zero case, and a rejected case expose different mistakes. Later lessons will translate this same input→work→output model into programs.
outcomes: Separate inputs, processing and outputs.
State input assumptions and a boundary case.

Assumption: distance and rate are nonnegative.

concepts.title: Write Precise Pseudocode
concepts.summary: Describe order and decisions without language-specific syntax.
explanation: Pseudocode is a readable plan, not a compiler input. Use clear commands such as READ, IF, DISPLAY and END. Indent the steps inside a decision so the reader knows which work is conditional.
Make comparison boundaries explicit. IF count > 0 excludes zero; IF count >= 0 includes it. Name what happens on invalid input. Do not hide required work behind phrases like “process the data.”
Dry-run the plan with a small input table before implementing it. Record the output that each input should produce. That table becomes the program’s acceptance cases later.
outcomes: Write ordered, unambiguous steps.
Dry-run valid, zero and invalid inputs.

worked_example.text:
READ count, price
IF count > 0
  DISPLAY count * price
ELSE
  DISPLAY Invalid count
END

concepts.title: Repair the First Compiler Error
concepts.summary: Read location and message, then make the smallest repair.
explanation: A compiler message names a source file, a line and a reason. The first error often causes later errors. Start there, compare punctuation and braces, and compile again before changing anything else.

Syntax errors stop compilation. A valid program can still contain a logic error: printing the wrong text compiles perfectly. Distinguish compiler success, runtime success, and meeting a requirement. The course saves them separately.
For missing semicolons, the compiler may point at the next line because that is where it can no longer parse the preceding statement. Look just above the reported location too.
outcomes: Separate syntax and logic errors.
Repair a compiler diagnostic without rewriting working code.

concepts.title: Values, Types & Variables
concepts.summary: Store related values and calculate a ticket total.
explanation: A variable has a declared type, a name and a current value. int stores whole numbers; double stores floating-point numbers; boolean stores true or false; char stores one UTF-16 code unit; String stores text. Choose the type from the meaning and range, not from the appearance of one example.

Assignment uses = and replaces the stored value. It does not assert equality. Declare a local variable before using it and assign a value before reading it. Double quotes delimit a String; single quotes delimit a char.

For a ticket receipt, give quantity and unit price readable names, multiply them, then print the result. double is useful for this introduction to decimal arithmetic, but binary floating point is not exact money accounting. The capstone uses bounded whole-number quantities instead.

Read and update a variable without confusing = with equality.

concepts.title: Names That Explain the Code
concepts.summary: Use valid identifiers and distinguish scope from spelling.
explanation: An identifier names a class, variable or method. In the simple names used here, start with a letter or underscore and continue with letters, digits or underscores. A name cannot be a Java keyword such as class or int. Java names are case-sensitive: total and Total are different names.

Prefer lowerCamelCase for variables and methods, and UpperCamelCase for classes. Naming conventions improve readability; they are not the same as compiler rules. Avoid cryptic one-letter names except small familiar counters.

Use a name that describes the value and, when needed, its unit: distanceKm or priceCents. A correct spelling does not make an undeclared variable available. More detailed scope rules come with methods.
outcomes: Identify a valid non-keyword identifier.
Name a value so another reader can understand its purpose.

concepts.title: Escapes Inside Java Strings
concepts.summary: Create newlines, tabs, quotes and backslashes deliberately.
explanation: A backslash inside a Java String introduces an escape. \n means a newline, \t a tab, \" a quote, and \\ one backslash. These are source characters interpreted by Java; they are not extra source-file line breaks.

Do not double an escape accidentally. The Java source "A\nB" prints two lines; source "A\\nB" prints the literal characters A, backslash, n, B. The editor must store real line breaks between source statements while preserving intended escapes inside Strings.
Tabs align to tab stops, not to a fixed number of visible spaces. For a carefully aligned table, use formatting later. For this exercise, exact tab characters are part of the required output.
outcomes: Distinguish source newlines from String escapes.
Print quotes, tabs and backslashes correctly.

walkthrough: \n inside the second String adds a row.

concepts.title: Arithmetic Without Truncation Surprises
concepts.summary: Group expressions and choose the calculation type before dividing.
explanation: Multiplication, division and remainder have higher precedence than addition and subtraction. Parentheses state the intended grouping. (a + b) / 2 computes an average; a + b / 2 computes a different expression.

When both operands are int, division produces an integer result truncated toward zero. Storing that result in a double afterward does not restore the lost fraction. Make an operand double before dividing, for example / 2.0.

For whole nonnegative quantities, % gives the remainder after division. Division by zero with integers throws an error; a guard will be taught with decisions. This early task uses fixed nonzero divisors, so it does not require untaught branch syntax.
outcomes: Trace expression precedence and parentheses.
Avoid integer division when a fractional result is required.

concepts.title: Update a Stored Value
concepts.summary: Trace += and increments without losing the old value.
explanation: total += amount updates total using its current value. For these int examples it behaves like total = total + amount. Other arithmetic compound assignments work similarly. Compound assignment has an implicit conversion to the left-hand type; do not use it to hide an inappropriate type choice.

count++ increments count. As a stand-alone statement, ++count has the same final effect. Inside an expression, postfix returns the old value and prefix returns the new one. Prefer separate update statements while learning, so the order stays visible.
A counter tracks how many operations happened. An accumulator tracks a combined result such as a sum. Both need an initial value before any update; upcoming loops will repeat these operations.
outcomes: Trace an accumulator before and after updates.
Distinguish prefix and postfix values in a small expression.

concepts.title: Tokens, Lines & an Input Guard
concepts.summary: Avoid leftover newlines and reject a wrong numeric token.
explanation: nextInt reads a numeric token but leaves the line ending after it. A following nextLine consumes the remaining portion of that line, which can be empty. If you intentionally mix these methods, consume that remainder once before reading the next full line.

hasNextInt checks whether the next token can be read as int, without consuming it. A small guard uses if (condition) { valid work } else { invalid work }. Only the true branch runs. This introduces the branch form needed for safe input; the decisions stage will deepen it.

This guard reports invalid input and ends this run. It does not retry yet. The loops stage adds retry and exit behavior. Supplying fewer lines than the stated contract is still a different error from a nonnumeric token.
outcomes: Explain the leftover-line pitfall.
Guard one numeric read instead of allowing an input mismatch crash.

walkthrough: An invalid token follows the else branch.

explanation: The first practical milestone accepts one ticket count per line, computes a total for each valid request, and repeats until q or EOF. The unit price is 120. Counts are whole numbers from 1 through 1000, keeping the bounded int multiplication safe.

Separate conversion failures from range failures in your reasoning, even when the required user message is the same. A rejected request must not produce a total or terminate future valid requests. Use whole-line reads so no invalid token is left behind.

Plan a test table before implementation: normal count, smallest count, zero, negative, trailing junk, overflow, valid request after an error, quit and EOF. Passing only one convenient request is not enough. This version is intentionally one main method; the next stage refactors it.

concepts.title: Small Methods with Inputs & Results
concepts.summary: Give a reusable operation a clear contract.
explanation: A method groups an operation under a name. Parameters describe the inputs it receives. A return type describes the value it produces; return sends that value to the caller and ends the method. void means no returned value.

Our first helper methods are static so main can call them without constructing an object. Define them inside Main but outside main. A method call does not automatically display its return value; the caller chooses whether to print or store it.

Keep calculation separate from input and printing. A total(count, unitPrice) method can then serve both a ticket workflow and a parcel workflow. Its contract should state valid inputs; validation may belong to the caller or the method, but the responsibility must be explicit.

Use a returned value without coupling calculation to console input.

concepts.title: Scope & Pass-by-Value
concepts.summary: Know which variable a method can actually change.
explanation: Local variables belong to their declaring block or method. A parameter is local to the called method. Two methods can each have a variable named value without sharing that local storage.

Java passes argument values by value. For int, the helper receives a copy of the integer value. Assigning a parameter or returning a new value does not update the caller’s local variable unless the caller stores that returned value.

For objects, Java still passes a copied reference value, not the caller’s variable itself. Object state can be mutated through a copied reference; object lessons will show that separately. Do not describe Java as pass-by-reference.

concepts.title: Specific Failures, Useful Recovery
concepts.summary: Catch what you can handle without hiding programming errors.
explanation: An exception interrupts the normal path. A matching catch handles it; execution does not resume at the failed statement. Catch close to a boundary where you can choose a useful response, such as converting a user-entered line.

NumberFormatException is a subtype of IllegalArgumentException. If you need distinct messages, catch the more specific type first. A broad superclass catch placed first would make the subtype catch unreachable.

Catch a conversion problem to let the next request run. Do not catch Exception around everything and print Success: that hides programming mistakes and file failures. Resource cleanup belongs in try-with-resources for closable file handles, which the persistence stage will teach.
outcomes: Trace which specific catch handles a failure.
Preserve useful errors and continue after recoverable bad input.

concepts.title: Test the Rule, Not Your Hope
concepts.summary: Use normal, boundary and failure cases to locate a logic defect.
explanation: A useful test records input, expected output, actual output and the reason the case matters. Derive expected results from the requirement before looking at your program. Otherwise you risk approving the same misunderstanding twice.

For a threshold at five items, test four, five and six. A wrong > versus >= may pass a middle case and fail the exact boundary. Reduce a failure to the smallest input that exposes it, trace the relevant values, and repair one cause.

Regression tests keep earlier behavior correct after a repair. Passing supplied checks does not prove all inputs correct. Add a new case when you discover a defect and explain the requirement it protects.

concepts.title: Arrays & a First-Match Search
concepts.summary: Store a fixed group and search without crossing its bounds.
explanation: An array has a fixed length and zero-based positions. new int[n] allocates n int slots initialized to zero. Access only indices from 0 through length - 1. The length field has no parentheses.

A linear search checks each position until it finds a match. Use -1 to represent no match when valid positions begin at zero. Stop at the first matching position when the contract asks for the first match; duplicates make that rule important.

An empty array is valid and has length zero. Its traversal loop must execute zero times. Do not read values[0] as an initial assumption when n can be zero. The input contract for this exercise supplies n and all required valid tokens.

Return a first matching index or a no-match sentinel.

concepts.title: A Resizable List of Titles
concepts.summary: Add, traverse and distinguish size from capacity.
explanation: ArrayList<String> stores a resizable sequence of String references. The type argument says what the list accepts. Use add to append, get(index) to read a position, size() for the element count and isEmpty() for the empty case.
Unlike an array, a list can grow as records arrive. Its size is the current number of elements, not an exposed backing-array capacity. Valid indices still run from 0 to size() - 1.

An enhanced for loop, for (String title : titles), visits each current element in order when you do not need its index. Avoid structural removal while using that loop. For removal by index, remember that later elements shift left and a numeric argument chooses the index overload.
outcomes: Use a typed resizable collection.

concepts.title: Records with Their Own State
concepts.summary: Construct distinct objects instead of parallel unrelated values.
explanation: A class defines fields and behavior for a kind of object. An object is one instance with its own state. new Item(title, quantity) invokes a constructor to initialize that instance. this.title refers to the field of the current object when a parameter has the same name.

Two distinct new objects have separate fields. Assigning Item b = a copies a reference, not the object. Then a and b refer to the same Item, so changing its mutable quantity through one reference is visible through the other.

For the single-file Studio runner, Item is a static nested class inside Main. That arrangement avoids additional public source files; it does not change Java’s pass-by-value rule. The next lesson controls state through methods.

concepts.title: Keep an Object Valid
concepts.summary: Put validation next to the state it protects.
explanation: Encapsulation puts a state rule behind an object’s interface. A private quantity field is accessed through getQuantity and updated through setQuantity, which rejects values outside 0..1000 before assigning. A constructor should enforce the same invariant.

A failed update must leave the previous state intact. Validate first, assign second. Do not partially mutate an object and then report an error. A final title reference cannot be reassigned after initialization.

Private access in Java includes the enclosing class’s nestmates; Main can technically access fields of its nested Item. We use getters/setters deliberately here as an interface discipline. In a separate top-level class, unrelated callers cannot directly access those private fields.

concepts.title: Milestone: an In-Memory Record Manager
concepts.summary: Combine objects, a list, methods and command recovery.
explanation: The command format is add|title|quantity, list, or q, one per line. Titles are trimmed, case-sensitive, unique, nonempty and at most 20 UTF-16 code units. Quantities are whole numbers 0..1000. Listing preserves insertion order and prints Empty for no records.

String.split takes a regular expression. To split on a literal |, the Java String must contain an escaped regex separator: split("\\|", -1). The -1 retains trailing empty fields so add|Orbit| is recognized as invalid data rather than a different shape.

Use an Item object for each record and ArrayList<Item> for the collection. A find method can return a matching Item or null. Use list and validation methods to keep command parsing from swallowing all the logic.

This milestone stores only in memory: exiting loses the records. The persistence stage adds a documented file format and makes restarting part of the test contract. Do not claim persistence for this version.

concepts.title: Append & Close a File Handle
concepts.summary: Use try-with-resources and explicit append options.
explanation: Some file APIs give you an open reader or writer. try (resource declaration) closes an AutoCloseable resource when the block exits, even on failure. Closing the writer flushes buffered data and releases the handle.

Keep success output after the try-with-resources block. A failure while writing or closing must not be reported as a successful append. This program accepts one line per run; multiple runs share the file only in a persistent workspace.

concepts.title: Milestone: Records That Survive Restart
concepts.summary: Save a documented format and prove that a new process can load it.
explanation: Build on the in-memory manager with save. records.txt is UTF-8 with one title|quantity record per line, no header, insertion order, case-sensitive unique titles, and quantities 0..1000. Missing file means an empty first run. An empty file is a valid empty inventory.

An existing malformed file is different from a missing file. Load validates every row and rejects duplicate titles, bad quantities, empty fields and bad shapes. On any load problem print Load failed and stop without saving. Keep the original file for inspection.

save serializes the current list with StringBuilder, writes a temporary sibling file, then replaces records.txt. Try an atomic move where supported, with a replace-move fallback. Finally remove the temporary file if it remains. This staging reduces the risk of truncating a good file during a failed write; it is not a full transactional database.

q does not autosave. An explicit save prints Saved or Save failed. Restart testing means two separate Java processes with the same working directory: add/save/quit in the first, list/quit in the second. Reading from the same in-memory object is not a restart test.
